analysis.one_liner: Creates an OSHA construction safety office, mandates on-site safety programs and specialists, and raises criminal penalties for deadly violations.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 26 bipartisan cosponsors, was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and its Health and Safety Subcommittee in 1989 and never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a dedicated construction safety office inside OSHA, required every covered contractor to maintain a written safety program, a site-specific hazard plan, and a certified safety specialist on site with authority to stop dangerous work, and required 24-hour reporting and federal investigation of serious injuries, deaths, and structural collapses. It also raised criminal penalties so an employer whose willful violation killed a worker could face up to 10 years in prison, or 20 for a repeat offense. It was sent to a House subcommittee in June 1989 and never advanced any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers, who face some of the highest fatality rates of any industry — from falls, trench collapses, and structural failures. The bill would have given them a trained safety professional on every large site with power to stop imminent dangers, guaranteed federal investigation of serious accidents within 24 hours, public reports on what happened, and real criminal consequences for employers who willfully ignored safety rules and got someone hurt or killed. The public also gains access to accident narratives and recommendations for preventing repeats.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an Office of Construction, Safety, Health, and Education inside OSHA with additional inspectors, and directs inspections to concentrate on the sites and employers with the highest potential for fatalities and serious injuries, with no advance notice to anyone.

Requires employers to report serious injuries, fatalities, and structural or potential collapses within 24 hours, and requires OSHA to inspect the site within 24 hours of that report, then publish a public narrative of what happened and how to prevent a repeat.

Requires contractors to maintain written safety and health programs, project-specific hazard analyses, accident records, and a certified construction safety specialist on site who can order hazards eliminated and stop work in an imminent danger.

Raises criminal penalties for willful safety violations: up to 5 years in prison for causing serious injury and up to 10 years for causing a worker's death, doubling to 10 and 20 years for repeat offenders, and extends liability to reckless conduct showing extreme indifference to human life.

Creates a Construction Safety and Health Training Academy to train federal inspectors and certify safety specialists, and gives workers and their representatives a right to request — and get a written answer to — an evaluation of any hazard or harmful substance on site.

analysis.who_pays: Construction contractors and the owners who hire them. They would bear the cost of hiring and retaining certified safety specialists, writing and maintaining safety programs and site plans, training every worker and supervisor, keeping detailed accident records, reporting incidents within 24 hours, and preserving evidence after accidents — plus the new risk of prison time for willful violations that injure or kill. Taxpayers would fund the new OSHA office, additional inspectors, and the training academy, subject to annual appropriations.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are substantial and fall hardest on small contractors: written company-wide programs, site-specific plans with hazard analyses, training records for every employee, and a qualified safety specialist on covered worksites. The bill itself acknowledges this burden by requiring a small business liaison within the new office and letting the Labor Secretary exempt certain small or unusual projects, provided they meet alternative safety requirements.

The bill layers significant new federal paperwork onto every covered project — pre-work notices with project cost and staffing estimates, annual incident reports even when nothing happened, and standard forms — a real cost that an honest supporter would have to weigh against the safety gains.

The specialist certification regime (a 40-hour course plus 18 months of supervised on-the-job training, or equivalent) and the new academy would be funded by taxpayers and could raise the price of construction and shrink the pool of eligible safety personnel, at least in the early years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but concentrated and quantifiable: administrative work, a salaried safety specialist, and training, offset in the bill by small-business exemptions, a compliance-assistance liaison, and federal training support. The benefits are harder to price because they are measured in deaths and crushing injuries prevented on an industry that loses workers to falls and trench collapses every year, and in criminal penalties that for the first time carried meaningful prison time for willful violations. The design is thoughtful rather than sweeping — prioritized inspections, no advance notice, written answers when a worker flags a hazard — so the main honest objection is cost and paperwork, not futility. On balance, the burden falls on the parties profiting from construction work while the protection goes to the people on the scaffolding.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Labor Committee and then to its Health and Safety Subcommittee in June 1989, and no one ever brought it to a markup or a vote before the two-year Congress ran out.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Shays, a Connecticut Republican, introduced the bill on May 4, 1989, joined by five original cosponsors including several fellow members of the Connecticut delegation.
The bill gathered 26 cosponsors — 19 Democrats and 7 Republicans — giving it bipartisan but modest support.
The House Committee on Education and Labor received the bill on May 4, 1989, and referred it to the Subcommittee on Health and Safety on June 9, 1989.
No markup, no vote, and no further action of any kind followed; the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, with the bill still sitting at the subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction contractors and developers are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory on-site safety specialists, written safety programs and hazard plans, 24-hour incident reporting, and prison exposure for willful violations that hurt or kill workers. Construction workers got none of the protections the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction contractors who avoided new rules

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Construction Safety, Health, and Education Improvement Act of 1989 on May 4, 1989, with five original cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 4, 1989, and referred it to a subcommittee; the full committee never scheduled a markup or vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and Safety
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 9, 1989, and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Its 26 cosponsors split 19 Democrats and 7 Republicans, but no committee or floor vote was ever taken, so no voting pattern exists to judge the fight by.

industries.note: They would have had to hire certified safety specialists, write and maintain safety programs and site-specific hazard plans, train all workers, report serious incidents within 24 hours, and face up to 10 years — 20 for repeat offenses — in prison for willful violations that kill a worker. The bill's entire cost side falls here, which is why the industry's interest ran against the protections workers would gain.

The bill defined owners as parties with control of property being built on and gave OSHA authority to prioritize inspecting projects of owners with worse-than-average injury records, adding oversight and potential delay. Developers avoided all of this when the bill died.

industries.industry: Occupational safety consulting and training providers
industries.note: Mandatory certified safety specialists on covered sites, a 40-hour certification course, triennial refreshers, and a federal training academy would have created a large new market for safety training and staffing. Their gain tracks directly with the safety protections workers would receive.

The bill would have given OSHA a dedicated construction office, additional inspectors, a training academy, mandatory 24-hour accident investigations, and a separately itemized construction budget line, expanding its reach into one of the deadliest industries.
